nameStory: St. John's Wort gets its name from its traditional bloom time around June 24th, the feast day of St. John the Baptist in Christian tradition. The word 'wort' is an old English term meaning 'plant' or 'herb,' often used for plants with medicinal properties. For centuries, people have gathered this sunny yellow flower during midsummer, believing it held special healing powers.
description: Common St. John's Wort is a cheerful perennial herb that brightens New England roadsides and fields with clusters of bright yellow flowers from late spring through summer. This hairless plant typically grows 1-3 feet tall with a bushy, upright habit and woody roots that help it spread. Its small oval leaves appear to have tiny holes punched through them when held up to the light, and its five-petaled yellow flowers are dotted with distinctive black spots along the petal edges. Though considered invasive in many areas, it's become a familiar sight across the region's disturbed soils and sunny openings.

idTips.label: Growth Habit

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem, completely hairless and smooth to the touch with a slightly waxy feel

habitat: Look for Common St. John's Wort in sunny, well-drained areas throughout New England, especially along roadsides, old fields, pastures, and disturbed soils. It thrives in open meadows, hillsides, and the edges of woods where it gets plenty of sunlight. This adaptable plant tolerates poor soils and establishes readily in areas where the ground has been disturbed by human activity or natural events.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as reddish shoots in late spring, quickly developing the characteristic opposite leaves with their translucent dots. Early flower buds begin forming at stem tips by late May.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from June through August, with clusters of bright yellow flowers creating showy displays. This is the best time for identification when both the perforated leaves and black-dotted flowers are clearly visible.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and develop into small capsules that split open to release seeds. The plant begins to yellow and die back, though some basal leaves may persist in protected areas.
seasonality.winter: Most above-ground parts die back to woody roots underground. Dead stems may persist, showing the branching pattern and dried seed capsules that help with identification.

funFact: When you crush the flowers and leaves of St. John's Wort between your fingers, they'll stain your skin bright red or purple - this 'blood' was once thought to represent the blood of St. John the Baptist and added to the plant's mystical reputation in folk medicine.
confusionNotes: St. John's Wort can be confused with other yellow wildflowers like wild mustards or buttercups, but the translucent leaf dots are a dead giveaway - hold any suspected leaf up to bright light and look for those tiny 'holes.' No other common yellow flower in New England has this perforated leaf feature.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its long history in herbal medicine and current use as an over-the-counter supplement for mild depression, St. John's Wort is considered an invasive species in much of New England. It can be toxic to livestock and interferes with many prescription medications, so it's a plant to observe and identify rather than harvest.
compareHints: Common St. John's Wort is distinguished from other New England Hypericum species by its relatively large size, prominent black dots on flower petals, and distinctly perforated leaves. Spotted St. John's Wort has black dots on leaves rather than just flowers, while smaller species like Dwarf St. John's Wort have much tinier flowers and grow closer to the ground. The translucent leaf glands are most pronounced in Common St. John's Wort compared to its relatives.
